方響以槌敲擊懸掛的長方形金屬音片發聲，音色清亮，音高依音片厚度漸變：較厚者音低，: The fangxiang sounds by striking suspended rectangular metal bars with a hammer; the timbre is clear, and the pitch changes with the thickness of the bars: thicker bars sound lower, thinner ones higher. Its range is about an octave and a half, with all the semitones within one octave, while the upper octave has no semitones. Unlike the modern metallophone, the fangxiang's bars are all the same length and width; different pitches are obtained mainly by adjusting the thickness, or by grinding thin the centre of the back of the bar.
方響始於南北朝梁代（502—557），隋唐時定型，多用於宮廷音樂；唐宋盛行，入十: The fangxiang began in the Liang dynasty of the Northern and Southern Dynasties (502–557) and took its fixed form in the Sui and Tang, when it was used mostly in court music; it was common in the Tang and Song, entering the qingyue and yanyue of the ten-part repertoire, and in the Song the imperial music bureau used it as a tuning instrument. It also reached the Korean peninsula and Japan. In the Tang there were famous players Xianqi Ma and Bing Wu, and the poets Li Yun and Lu Guimeng wrote lyrics to be accompanied by the fangxiang. In the Qing it was still used in court ritual music: in the triumphal song the mounted guard of honour each held one piece and struck it. In the 1980s it was enlarged to fifty-one keys with equal temperament and two rows, the upper row in C♯ and the lower in C major, on a stand that could be raised and lowered, for accompanying Chinese traditional orchestras.
方響實際用於中國宮廷禮樂與燕樂，唐代十部伎的清樂、燕樂及宋代教坊定律皆用之；清代: The fangxiang was actually used in Chinese court ritual and banquet music: qingyue and yanyue in the ten-part repertoire of the Tang, and tuning in the Song imperial music bureau. In the Qing the triumphal song was struck by mounted guardsmen each holding one piece. It also reached Korea, where it is still used in Korean court music. In modern times it can be heard accompanying Chinese traditional orchestras, for example in The Great Wall Capriccio, where it imitates bells; the American composer Lou Harrison also used it in works for violin and various instruments.
方響是中國傳統金屬體鳴敲擊樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號111.22: The fangxiang is a Chinese metal idiophone percussion instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.222, classed as 'metal' in the eight-sound system. It consists of sixteen rectangular tuned bars, mostly of iron or bronze, hung in two rows of eight on a frame; the bars rest at an angle on iron pegs wrapped with felt, and are struck in the centre with a hammer, so it can play a melody. It began in the Liang dynasty, became a common instrument of court music after the Sui and Tang, and appears in the qingyue and yanyue of the ten-part repertoire of the Tang and in Song imperial tuning.

方響發聲體為十六片長方形音片，來源載有鐵、銅或玉；音片長度、面積相同，以磨薄背面: The sounding body is sixteen rectangular bars, which the source gives as iron, bronze or jade; the bars are the same length and the same area, and the pitch is adjusted by grinding thin the centre of the back. The bars rest on two horizontal iron pegs wound with yellow felt. The player strikes the centre of the bar with a pair of small hammers. The source does not state the material of the frame or of the rest of the body.
演奏時將十六片音片分上下兩層懸於架上，使音片斜依鐵鋌，再以一副小槌敲擊音片中央發: Hang the sixteen bars in two tiers on the frame, resting them at an angle on the iron pegs, and strike the centre of the bars with a pair of small hammers. A beginner first learns where the bars hang and where to strike, keeping the bars steady at the node; then play bar by bar with a hammer in each hand, practising melodic lines from low to high and from high to low.
